title: "Repository Structure and Metadata"

# Repository Structure and Metadata

A package manager cannot download thousands of individual packages just to discover what software exists or resolve dependencies. Instead, it queries a centralized index file called **repository metadata**.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|               HTTP / HTTPS Web Server (Nginx)             |
|                                                           |
|  /repo/x86_64/                                            |
|  ├── repodata.json (or Packages.gz / core.db.tar.gz)      |
|  ├── repodata.json.sig (GPG / minisign detached signature)|
|  ├── curl-8.5.0-1-x86_64.pkg                              |
|  ├── openssl-3.2.1-1-x86_64.pkg                           |
|  └── zlib-1.3.1-1-x86_64.pkg                              |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
                              |
                     HTTPS GET repodata.json
                              |
                              v
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|                   Client Package Manager                  |
|                                                           |
| 1. Verifies GPG signature against trusted distribution key|
| 2. Parses local cache of repository metadata              |
| 3. Computes dependency graph & presents transaction plan  |
| 4. Downloads only required package binaries               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
```

## Repository Metadata Schemas

### 1. Debian (`Packages.gz` and `Release`)
In a Debian repository, the `Packages` file contains the concatenated `control` stanzas of every package in the pool, along with SHA256 checksums, package file sizes, and filesystem paths. The `Release` file contains the cryptographic hashes of the `Packages` files and is signed with the distribution maintainer's private GPG key (`Release.gpg` or in-line `InRelease`).

### 2. Arch Linux (`core.db.tar.gz`)
In Arch repositories, `core.db.tar.gz` is a tarball containing one directory per package. Inside each directory are two files: `desc` (package description, version, size, dependencies) and `depends` (exact dependency version requirements). When `pacman -Sy` runs, it simply downloads this small archive and uncompresses it into `/var/lib/pacman/sync/core/`.

### 3. Modern JSON Metadata (Custom Distro Approach)
For our custom BYOL distribution, we can design a clean, modern metadata format using standard JSON:

```json
{
  "repository": "byol-core",
  "version": 1,
  "updated_at": "2026-10-29T12:00:00Z",
  "packages": {
    "curl": {
      "version": "8.5.0",
      "release": 1,
      "arch": "x86_64",
      "filename": "curl-8.5.0-1-x86_64.byol",
      "sha256": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
      "size": 492100,
      "depends": ["glibc>=2.38", "openssl>=3.0.0", "zlib>=1.3.0"]
    },
    "openssl": {
      "version": "3.2.1",
      "release": 1,
      "arch": "x86_64",
      "filename": "openssl-3.2.1-1-x86_64.byol",
      "sha256": "4a5e1e...39f1",
      "size": 3410290,
      "depends": ["glibc>=2.38"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Cryptographic Signing of Metadata

Never distribute packages over plain HTTP without cryptographic authentication. If an attacker performs a Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) attack or compromises a mirror server, they could tamper with package payloads.

Signing workflow:
```bash
# Generate detached cryptographic signature using minisign or gpg:
$ minisign -Sm repodata.json -s /etc/byol/keys/distro.key

# Client verifies signature before trusting metadata:
$ minisign -Vm repodata.json -p /etc/byol/keys/distro.pub
Signature and comment signature verified
```
